opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I'd say it was a mix of the right instinct and some naive assumptions.

The instinct was right in the sense that in autonomous driving, we'd already learned the hard way that you can't collect enough real-world data to cover the long tail. Simulation was how we stress-tested the system: generating corner cases, replaying scenarios, scaling up evaluation without putting cars on the road. So when I moved toward embodied intelligence, it felt natural to think, okay, robots have an even worse data problem, so simulation should be even more valuable here.

But what I underestimated was how different the core difficulty is. In driving, the hardest part of simulation is mostly about the behavior of other agents and the perception side: rendering sensors realistically, modeling how pedestrians and other drivers act. The physics of the car itself is relatively well understood. In manipulation, it's almost the opposite. The physics *is* the problem. Contact, friction, deformable objects, cables, cloth, liquids. The moment a gripper touches something, the sim-to-real gap opens up in ways that are very hard to close just by making the simulator more accurate.

So my first attempt was, in a way, too much of a direct transplant. I tried to bring over the pipeline mindset: build a high-fidelity world, generate massive scenarios, train and evaluate at scale. What I learned is that for embodied tasks, you need to be much more thoughtful about what simulation is actually good for. It's very useful for things like locomotion, for pretraining certain representations, for evaluation and safety checks. But for fine-grained manipulation, real data, or some clever mix of real and synthetic, often matters more than I expected.

I don't regret it, though. That attempt forced me to really understand where the boundary of simulation lies, and that understanding shaped everything we did afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, looking back, that first attempt was a bit naive. When I came out of autonomous driving, I had this very strong belief that simulation was the key to everything. In driving we had spent years building sim pipelines, closed-loop testing, scenario generation, all of it, and it genuinely worked. So my instinct was simple: robots are just cars with more joints. Take the same stack, swap the vehicle model for a humanoid or an arm, and you're done.

That turned out to be wrong in a few important ways.

The first thing I underestimated was contact. In driving, the physics you care about is mostly rigid-body dynamics on a flat surface, tire friction, and perception. Those are hard, but they're tractable and relatively well understood. In manipulation, everything is about contact. Grasping a cup, folding cloth, opening a drawer that sticks a little. The gap between what a simulator tells you and what actually happens with a real gripper on a real object is enormous. We spent months tuning a sim that looked beautiful, and then the robot would fail on a plastic bottle because the friction model was slightly off.

The second thing was data. In driving, the long tail is in the scenarios, not the physics. You can generate a million variations of a pedestrian stepping off a curb, and the simulator is faithful enough that training on them transfers. In embodied intelligence, the long tail is in the physical world itself: object diversity, deformation, lighting on reflective surfaces. Simulation helps, but it doesn't substitute for real interaction data the way it does in driving.

And the third thing, which I think I only understood later, is that the role of simulation changes. In driving it's primarily a validation and safety tool. In embodied intelligence it's much more of a training environment, especially for reinforcement learning for locomotion. So the engineering priorities are completely different. You care less about photorealism and perfect scenario coverage, and much more about throughput, parallelism, and domain randomization.

So I wouldn't say the attempt failed, but I'd say I transferred the wrong things. The mindset transferred well, the discipline of closed-loop evaluation, the obsession with the sim-to-real gap. The actual tooling, much less so. If I were to do it again, I'd spend the first three months just working with the physical robot before writing a single line of simulation code, so I'd know what actually needed simulating.

r001.rationale: He says his initial belief that simulation was key and that robots were essentially cars with more joints was wrong, then identifies contact physics and real interaction data as distinct embodied-intelligence challenges.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe it as an attempt to understand which parts of my autonomous-driving simulation experience could carry over. There’s a clear connection: in both cases, an intelligent system has to perceive its surroundings, make decisions, and act, and simulation gives you a way to test that process repeatedly.

But I wouldn’t assume that experience transfers directly. With embodied intelligence, especially manipulation, contact and physical interaction become central. A simulation can look convincing while still getting the details that determine whether an action succeeds wrong.

So my initial approach would be to start with a narrow task and close the loop: does something learned or tested in simulation actually work in the physical world? To me, that’s the useful measure—not how elaborate the simulator is, but whether it helps us make real progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a useful starting point, but also a process of discovering where the analogy breaks down. My initial thought was that autonomous driving already involves an agent perceiving an environment, making decisions, and acting, so some of that simulation experience should transfer to embodied intelligence.

But once you move toward manipulation and more varied physical tasks, the demands change. Contact, friction, and small errors in an object’s position can determine whether an action succeeds. So the question becomes less about how realistic the simulation looks and more about whether it captures the interactions the agent needs to learn.

For me, the value of that first attempt was establishing a way to approach the problem: use simulation to test ideas efficiently, then examine carefully which capabilities transfer to the real world and where the gaps remain.
